dialog.body: Public Works, storm line, this is Lorraine. How can I help you?

Oh, good, somebody picked up. I wasn't sure, it being Saturday and City Hall's closed, I figured I'd get a machine or... Anyway. I'm calling about the drain on our corner. The storm drain. It backed up and we got water in the basement, and I've been meaning to call since Thursday but I didn't know who...
Okay, no, you got the right place. This line's open on the weekends for exactly this kind of thing. So you've got a drain that backed up and water in the basement. Can I start with the address?

Twenty-five Howard Street. In the Fifth Ward, near the corner there, the drain's right at the corner, you can't miss it. Well, you could miss it, actually, that's the whole problem, you can't even see it under all the leaves...
Twenty-five Howard Street. Okay. And your name?
Lucille Fiore. F-I-O-R-E.
F-I-O-R-E. Lucille Fiore, 25 Howard Street. Got it. So tell me what happened.

So it was that rain, the one that started Wednesday and just wouldn't quit, it went right through into Thursday. And sometime overnight, Wednesday night into Thursday, the eighteenth, the water came in through the window well. The glass, on the street side. The window down in the well. It just came right through around the glass and down the wall and onto the floor. My husband went down Thursday morning and he called up to me, he said, Lucille, there's water, and I thought he meant a little puddle, you know, from the...
And it wasn't a little puddle.
No. About two inches. Across the whole front of the basement. Two inches doesn't sound like much on the phone but when it's sitting there...

No, two inches is plenty. Let me read that back to you. Overnight Wednesday into Thursday, December eighteenth, water came in through the window well on the street side, through the glass, and you had about two inches in the basement. That right?
That's right. That's exactly it.
Is the basement finished at all? Carpet, walls, anything like that?

No, no, it's just a basement. Concrete floor, it's just storage. But that's where everything is. We had boxes down there of the kids' school things, report cards and drawings and, oh, all of that, I kept all of it. And they were sitting on the floor in the front, right under that window. The bottoms are soaked through. I don't know yet what's ruined, I haven't had the heart to go through them... And there's a spare refrigerator down there and that was sitting in the water too. I don't know if it works now. My husband unplugged it, he didn't want to touch it.
That's smart, leave it unplugged until it's good and dry. Okay, so boxes of the kids' school things got wet, and a spare refrigerator was sitting in the water. I'm putting that in the notes.

And here's the thing, and this is why I'm calling and not just mopping up and forgetting about it. That drain on the corner. The catch basin. It's been buried in leaves since, I don't know, the end of October? Early November? You walk by, you can't even see the grate. It's just a pile. And I kept thinking, somebody's going to come by with the truck, somebody's going to clean that off before it rains. Nobody did. So Wednesday the rain comes and the water's got nowhere to go. It just sat in the street and came up over the curb and right down into my window well. It's not like it's a mystery...
So the catch basin at the corner was covered over with leaves and the water couldn't get into it.

It couldn't get in. It had nowhere to go. I watched it Thursday morning, the street was like a pond from the corner right up to the front of my house. And this is a city drain. It's not mine, I can't go out there with a rake at seventy-seven years old and dig out a storm drain, that's... that's the city's job, isn't it? I pay my taxes. I've been in this house twenty-eight years. I love this street, I do, I'm not one of these people who calls about everything. But this, this shouldn't have happened.
No, I hear you. And you're right, the catch basins in the street are ours. That's not on you to clear.
Well somebody should have cleared it. That's all I'm saying. Weeks it sat there.
Understood. I'm going to write that the grate's been covered for weeks, since around the end of October, early November.
Put that in. Please. Because I don't want somebody to come out and look at it now, after, and say oh it looks fine. The rain washed some of it around but it's still covered, it's still...
I'll make sure it says that. Let me ask you, is there still any water in the street right now, or is it just the leaves?

It went down. Friday it went down. But it's still all piled up there, it's like a mat. You step on it, it's mushy. And they're saying more rain next week, aren't they? I heard something on the radio... I just, I can't go through this again before Christmas.
Okay. Can I ask, has anybody else on Howard Street said anything to you? Neighbors getting water too?

That's what I wanted to ask you, actually. Do you have any record, has anyone else called from our street? Because I can't be the only one. The house next to me, the one on the corner, they've got to have gotten something, they're even lower than I am...

Let me look. Give me one second. [pause] Okay, I'm searching Howard Street for this week. [pause] I'm not seeing anything else logged for Howard Street from this storm. That doesn't mean nobody else got water, it just means nobody's called it in to this line. We've had a lot of calls since Wednesday, all over the city, but nothing else on your street that I can see.
Nothing. Huh. Well, that figures. Everybody figures somebody else called. That's how it goes, isn't it. Everybody's waiting on everybody else and meanwhile the drain just sits there...

It happens a lot, honestly. So your call is going to be the one that gets it on the list. If your neighbors did get water, you might tell them to call too, because when we see a few reports from the same spot it carries more weight.

I'll tell them. I'll tell the people on the corner. But I shouldn't have to go knocking on doors to get a drain cleaned, you know? It should just get done. Every fall, the leaves come down, you'd think somebody would have it on a calendar...

I know. I'm going to put this in as a drain backup at the corner by 25 Howard Street, catch basin covered with leaves, water in the street and into your basement through the window well. And what I can do is get a crew scheduled to go check the corner and clear it.
When? Because Saturday, I know nobody's going out today...
I'm looking at the schedule. With everything that came in after this storm the weekend's spoken for, but I can get the corner on for Monday. Monday the twenty-second.
Monday. [pause] Okay. Monday. And they'll actually come Monday? Because I've been looking at that pile for weeks waiting for somebody to just come...
It's going on Monday's list. Morning or afternoon I can't tell you, they work through the list as they go, but it's on there for Monday the twenty-second.
All right. All right. I'll be watching for them, believe me. I'll be at the window.
I believe it. Can I get a phone number for you, so if the crew or the office needs to reach you about it?
It's the house phone. 401-555-0107.
401-555-0107. And that's the best number for you?
That's the only number. We just have the one. Somebody's always home.

Okay. Let me read the whole thing back so you know what I've got. Lucille Fiore, 25 Howard Street, Fifth Ward, phone 401-555-0107. Basement took on water overnight Wednesday into Thursday, December eighteenth, about two inches, came in through the glass of the window well on the street side. Boxes of the kids' school things and a spare refrigerator got wet. Catch basin at the corner has been buried in leaves for weeks and the water couldn't drain. Crew to check and clear the corner on Monday, December twenty-second. Anything I missed?
No, that's... that's it. That's all of it. Except, well, what about the boxes, the refrigerator? Is that, does the city...

So that part's not something I handle from this line. Damage claims go through a different office at City Hall, and they're closed till Monday. What I'd do is take pictures of everything now, the boxes, the refrigerator, where the water came in, before you throw anything out. Then call City Hall Monday and ask about filing a claim, and you can tell them you've got this report in with Public Works.
Pictures. Okay. My husband can do that, he's got the camera... I'll have him do it today. Before we move anything else.
That's a good idea. And keep your window well clear on your side if you can, but the corner, that's ours. That's what Monday's for.

I just want it fixed so it doesn't happen again. That's all I want. I'm not looking to make trouble. I've lived on this street twenty-eight years and I like it here, I like my neighbors, I like the city... But you can't let a drain go like that and then act surprised. You know?
I do know. And I've put your concerns in the notes, about it being covered so long. That'll go along with the work order.
Thank you. I appreciate you, you've been very patient with me, I know I go on...
You're fine. That's what I'm here for. If something changes before Monday, if it rains and the street starts filling up again, call this line back, it's open all weekend.
All weekend. Okay. I'll keep the number by the phone. Hopefully I won't need it...
Hopefully not. You take care, Mrs. Fiore. Get those pictures.
I will. Monday. Thank you, Lorraine. Bye now...
